Chordata. Comprising all vertebrates—mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish—alongside two invertebrate subphyla, Chordata is a major phylum of deuterostome animals containing the most complex and familiar animals, including humans. Chordates are defined by the presence of four distinctive features.

First is the notochord, a flexible rod-like structure extending along the back that provides skeletal support. In most adult vertebrates it's replaced by the vertebral column, but it remains the defining chordate characteristic. Second is a dorsal hollow nerve cord—a tube of nervous tissue located above the notochord that develops into the brain and spinal cord in vertebrates. Third are pharyngeal slits or pouches that appear during embryonic development. In fish they evolve into gill arches, but in terrestrial vertebrates they transform into elements of the jaw, inner ear, and neck.

Fourth is a muscular post-anal tail extending past the anus. It contains skeletal elements and muscles and is used for balance or propulsion, though it is reduced or lost in some adult forms. Chordates also feature an endostyle on the floor of the pharynx—or in vertebrates, its homologous descendant, the thyroid gland—which secretes mucus to trap food particles in filter-feeding invertebrate chordates.

Chordates divide into three subphyla. There's Vertebrata, containing vertebrates with backbones. There's Urochordata, the tunicates or sea squirts, which lose their notochord in adulthood. And there's Cephalochordata, the lancelets, which retain all chordate features throughout their entire lives.

Echinoderms are the closest major invertebrate relatives of chordates, sharing that deuterostome pattern of embryonic development. They compete with arthropods across terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. Phylum Chordata represents the lineage that produced the most complex nervous systems and skeletons in the animal kingdom, culminating in vertebrates.
